newsitem.title: USA: Reynolds leaves Alabama staffing to Alcoa.
newsitem.headline: Reynolds leaves Alabama staffing to Alcoa.

text.p: Reynolds Metals Co said any decision to lay off workers or close the Alabama rolling mill would be taken by Aluminum Co of America (Alcoa) as it takes over the complex sometime in the second half of this year.

Mike Jones, Reynolds' executive vice president of external affairs, said there had been confusion over the term "plant closure notice" when mentioned by the company to Wall Street analysts earlier this week.

The use of this term simply indicated to unions that Alcoa would not assume the existing multi-year labor contract in place at the Alabama plant, thereby triggering some enhanced benefits as the contract is revoked, Jones said.
"This got understood that we had given a warning notice that we were going to shut down the plant. That is not the case," Jones said.
"If we complete the sale, Alcoa and the union will negotiate a new contract," Jones added. "They want the option to look at the whole (labor) package."

"Alcoa are reviewing the situation and are going to decide between now and the time the deal is completed, what level of operations the want to run the plant at. What level of operations will be their decision going forward," Jones said.
"I don't think they have gone far enough into it to reach that decision yet," Jones added.
The Alabama Alloys plant employs 2,250 people.
Employees at the plant would be laid off as Reynolds employees when the deal is concluded. "The question is whether they are rehired as Alcoa employees," Jones said.
Reynolds said earlier this year it expected to realise an after-tax loss of $225 million to $250 million on the transaction.
The company also said it anticipated that future employment levels at Alabama would be reduced, perhaps substantially.
Substantial was defined later by Reynolds' vice chairman, J Wilt Wagner, as 500 or more jobs.
Reynolds said this week it believed U.S. Justice Department would approve the sale to Alcoa.
